What to Watch for in the 2026 U.S. Midterms

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

India Targets Journalists in Crackdown on Growing Protest Movement

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

Testing the Legal Limits of Press Access

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-15 14:51 UTC

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. This Newsroom Wants You to Be Part of the Journey Before It Even Starts

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-06 10:00 UTC

My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

America’s Shrinking Local Newsrooms, Through a Photographer’s Lens

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-02 12:30 UTC

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

Seven Takeaways on Convenience and News

Nieman Reports · 2026-09-25 14:53 UTC

"Against Convenience: Embracing Friction in an Age of Endless Ease" was released on Sept.15, 2026, by Hanover Square Press, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Courtesy of Hanover Square Press From the earliest pitch, I knew that I wanted to cover the news industry in my book, “Against Convenience.” The book looks at the technology around us and asks whether it’s really improving our lives. Is delivery food worth the higher price? Is streaming music better than collecting CDs or MP3s? News embodies the paradox of modern convenience: We have access to more information than ever before, but misinformation and partisanship are rampant and the purveyors of reliable information are struggling to stay solvent. Plus, I figured if I was going to criticize other fields — tech, entertainment, appliance manufacturing — I couldn’t avoid my own. I don’t know how interested the average nonjournalist is in the day-to-day operations of the news business, so I tried to look in the mirror more than gaze at my navel.

澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

EIA Today in Energy · 2026-10-16 14:00 UTC

We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country-California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida-are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives.

Stablecoins and the macroeconomy: Bank disintermediation versus fiscal space

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-02 00:00 UTC

Stablecoins compete with banks for households’ holdings of safe and liquid assets, while creating additional demand for government debt. Building on a novel quantitative macroeconomic model, this column discusses how widespread stablecoin adoption affects the macroeconomy. In the baseline scenario, large-scale adoption has small negative long-run output effects. However, the sign and size of the effect depend on fiscal parameters, the regulatory framework for stablecoin reserve holdings, and whether stablecoin demand and issuance originate domestically or abroad. Short-run output effects can be significantly positive as the fiscal space channel activates faster.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

When judges move markets: Ideological shifts in the Supreme Court and macroeconomic expectations

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-01 00:00 UTC

Courts increasingly shape economic policy. This column studies unexpected deaths of US Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court’s ideological balance. High-frequency asset price responses reveal that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower activity expectations, and lower bond yields. A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses. The findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court as news about future aggregate demand, in particular future fiscal policy.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

The boom before the bust: From the Roaring Twenties to the Great Depression

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-31 00:00 UTC

The investment boom in artificial intelligence technologies has raised concerns about a potential bubble. This column argues that the 1920s boom and the Great Depression offer useful lessons. During the 1920s, process innovation grew rapidly, while product innovation stagnated. In turn, process innovation fuelled an investment boom based on an expectation of future demand. When this expectation failed to materialise, a sharp contraction followed. Thus, the optimism and prosperity of the Roaring Twenties help explain the onset of the Great Depression, and offer a cautionary tale for today’s artificial intelligence boom.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Stablecoins as a vehicle for dollarisation: Evidence from capital controls and currency crises

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-31 00:00 UTC

Stablecoins could make payments and remittances cheaper and faster, but policymakers worry they could also help residents, particularly in emerging markets, circumvent capital controls and move savings into US dollars. This column introduces estimates of stablecoin flows and holdings for 188 countries, built from public blockchain data. Emerging market and developing economies take part in 86% of cross-border stablecoin flows and hold about three quarters of stablecoins. Cross-border stablecoin activity rises by roughly 30% after countries tighten restrictions on capital outflows and shows no sign of falling back when they are lifted. Holdings rise by roughly 75% in the year after a currency crisis begins and then persist.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Cooperatives in the 21st Century

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-30 00:00 UTC

Go to work, follow orders all day, and your living standards will rise. That is the deal behind the capitalist economy. In his forthcoming book, Cooperatives in the twenty-first century, Francesco Caselli (LSE, CEPR) argues that the deal has been broken for two generations. Pay at the top keeps climbing. Pay in the middle and at the bottom has barely moved. The usual fixes for spiralling inequality are higher taxes on the rich and stronger unions. Francesco's answer is to change who owns the firm. In a worker cooperative there are no outside shareholders, so the profits stay with the people who produce them. In conversation with Tim Phillips, he explains which of the economic objections to cooperatives are red herrings, and which ones are more serious.

Assessing China as a technological innovator

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-30 00:00 UTC

The dramatic rise of domestic patent publications by Chinese inventors has raised questions about the extent of Chinese innovations. This column uses a newly assembled dataset of Chinese patents to understand the Chinese innovative ecosystem. The data reveal an innovation system that is more broad-based, more university-centred, and less dominated by state-owned enterprises, large national champions, or US-trained returnees than many standard narratives suggest. The findings challenge preconceptions about where Chinese innovation is occurring and suggest the importance of better understanding the mechanisms behind central coordination and its impact.

Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Unraveling the Cobweb of Global Imbalances: Drivers, Vulnerabilities and Adjustment Scenarios -- by Stefan Avdjiev, Kristin Forbes, Tsvetelina Nenova, Marjorie Santos

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons). Valuation gains on international investment positions have supported economic growth in many countries since 2010, while also increasing their vulnerability to financial market adjustments.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Affirmative Action, Faculty Productivity and Caste Interactions: Evidence from Engineering Colleges in India -- by Robert W. Fairlie, Saurabh Khanna, Prashant Loyalka, Gagandeep S. Sachdeva

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Affirmative action programs are often criticized because of concerns that they result in lower worker productivity and efficiency losses. We study the relative productivity of workers benefiting from an aggressive affirmative action policy in a setting where hiring constraints are mandated upon employers and are typically likely to bind. In India, colleges are required to reserve approximately 50 percent of faculty hires for individuals from disadvantaged caste and social class groups. We collect and analyze data from a nationally representative sample of 50 engineering and technology colleges in India, some of which randomly assign students to classrooms. We find that reservation category faculty have lower levels of education, lower professorial ranks and fewer years of experience in academia than general category faculty who are not hired through reservations.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Income Inequality and Intergenerational Mobility in Russia: Trends, Sources, and Measurement -- by Kristina Butaeva, Steven N. Durlauf, Dmitry Rudenko

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata. It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested. Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race -- by Apoorva Babbar, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley, Jingyuan Zeng

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications.

A Gentle Guide to Boredom

LessWrong · 2026-11-02 12:53 UTC

It's the strangest feeling, isn't it? It reminds me of an emotion, but rather than residing in the heart, it's in the mind. How does it work for you? Perhaps you need to slow down enough to induce it in yourself, to gather accurate data on what is actually happening when you feel this way. To me, it feels as if my brain is searching for something to pay attention to, and is coming up short. It wants to be immersed, and is finding nothing it deems valuable to be immersed in. Sometimes when it's been long enough, I start feeling pained from being denied the state of mind I so desperately want to inhabit. Maybe I am pained by having to be within myself. It can be difficult to tell. I know a lot of people for whom their own company is the worst company they could have, so they try to do as much as they can to escape it. Being as young as you are, you might not have developed this desire to be free from yourself. But if this is something you relate to, you don't have to despair. Strangely, the very mind that we want to run away from can be shaped into what we desire.

Gaming (out) the system

LessWrong · 2026-11-02 09:52 UTC

Verification changes the stampede dynamics. I'm currently at FASR in the UK, it's an 8-week program dedicated to "compute verification". That's the not-quite-here-yet technology that would allow us to make agreements about how AI is being used, without leaking any closely-held secrets. You can think of it as "arms control for AI". Part of what I'm working on is the game theory of an agreement. This can get quite detailed (in terms of defining how often and how detailed an inspection should be) in order to make cooperation the best overall choice. But in this post I want to provide a high-level look at how verification would change the dynamics from "stampede" to "cooperate". Below I've got a map which allows us to use a player's value for Hazard (x-axis) and their value about how bad that incident might be (y-axis) as inputs, to see what their optimal strategy should be. Hazard here is the baseline chance that a project loses control of its ASI, even if they could take their time and think things through carefully. But, sadly, we don't live in a sane world.

What Vera Rubin observatory’s first new dwarf planet means

Big Think · 2026-11-02 07:00 UTC

Back in 2006, the International Astronomical Union controversially demoted Pluto. This composite image of Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, was based on photographs taken by the New Horizons mission as it flew by the Plutonian planetary system back in 2015. Charon’s appearance is vastly different from Pluto’s, but both bodies are shown with the correct relative size and albedo. The surface features on Pluto show evidence of recent changes, indicating that the next time we visit Pluto to image it at this level of precision, it may exhibit a remarkably different appearance. Credit: NASA, APL, SwRI As part of that process, they officially defined “planet” and “dwarf planet” for the first time. The scientific line between planetary (above) and non-planetary (below) status, for three potential definitions of an orbit-clearing phenomenon and a star equal to the mass of our Sun. This definition could be extended to every exoplanetary system we can imagine to determine whether a candidate body meets the criteria, as we’ve defined them, for being classified as a true planet or not.

Meal prep that works for me

LessWrong · 2026-11-02 06:44 UTC

I've always been somewhat disappointed in myself for not having "figured out" meal prep. "You're 33 years old", my inner critic will say. "Meal prep isn't complicated. There are a million resources available online. You've had years to learn and iterate. How haven't you figured it out by now?" Well, I finally may have something that works. One meal for dinner, another for breakfast. For dinner it is a bowl with brown rice, lentils, ground chicken, green peas, garlic, and spices. For breakfast it's a bowl with brown rice, black beans, taco seasoning, caramelized onions, egg whites, avocado, and a sauce. Before discussing each meal, let me begin by talking about what matters to me and how I prioritize things. Considerations I'm gonna admit something that sounds a little pathetic. I don't think I've ever said it out loud before. At least not loudly. I've built up an identity of a "foodie", and because of this identity, I feel a sense of embarrassment when the cooking I do is boring.

Against Against SURA

LessWrong · 2026-11-01 23:24 UTC

Scott: the Against SURA essay is well-written, but it is lacking on the merits. Do you think that at the current level of capabilities, six months would be sufficient to solve alignment of superintelligences? Maybe you think that 6 months would be sufficient in a year? You don’t spell this out; it would be great if you did. The race can be stopped. If the government had any idea what’s going on, it would be stopped already. Hell, if the *Chinese* government had any idea what’s going on, they’d stop the race: governments can stop unilaterally, then exercise all of their soft and hard power to stop others while using technology to avoid escalation. (See MAIM.) Among companies, one doesn’t even have to stop unilaterally; that wouldn’t help. They do need to stop lying to politicians and the public. They need to start saying what the situation is. They need to start advocating for everyone pausing simultaneously, and advocating for the governments to pause everyone on the planet. They’re not doing that.

Why smart people stay stuck in research mode

Big Think · 2026-10-30 19:19 UTC

I recently had coffee with a university colleague who told me she was in the middle of planning a workshop. She had bought a couple of books about hosting workshops, had created a spreadsheet projecting attendance under different scenarios, and was now comparing ticketing platforms. But she still hadn’t invited a single person. We talked about how none of that research was necessarily a waste of time. When you love learning, figuring out the best approach can be enjoyable in itself. But every answer can produce another question, and before you know it, preparation has become the project. Worse, that endless research keeps you busy while the harder questions wait: Will anybody be interested? Am I any good at this? The psychology of endless research You could call this a problem of overthinking, but research points instead to several nuanced and overlapping tendencies that can make gathering information feel easier, safer, and more satisfying than taking action. A better option could be hiding somewhere.

Ask Ethan: What should you do when a respected theory is false?

Big Think · 2026-10-30 06:00 UTC

At every point in our quest to understand the world and universe — the one around us and the one within us — we can only start based on what we know and can imagine at present. We are biased by what we know and what we’re ignorant of, and we’re also influenced by the range of experiences that we’re aware of. Nobody has access to the full suite of evidence that all of humanity has ever collected, and even that full suite of evidence doesn’t shed light on all that exists and is possible within our Universe. Our knowledge is limited, and our theories that we’ve devised to explain, predict, and model reality are limited in numerous ways as well. Even the very best of our best theories and ideas are far from complete, and in many instances, there are very popular, well-respected ideas in a variety of fields that are deeply flawed at best. So what can we do, and what should we do, when a respected theory runs up against a truth we’ve uncovered from our own lived experience? Was dark matter first discovered by Fritz Zwicky or Vera Rubin?

Big Think · 2026-10-29 06:00 UTC

It’s hard to believe, but the idea that the Universe was dominated not by normal matter but rather by dark matter — a novel form of non-interacting matter that’s completely distinct from protons, neutrons, and electrons — goes all the way back to 1933: nearly a full century ago. For decades, the overwhelming majority of the leading astronomers and physicists dismissed the idea as being ill-motivated and lacking sufficient evidence backing it, and it gained very little traction on both the theoretical and observational fronts throughout the 1930s, 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s. It was only with the novel results and improved instrumentation initially leveraged by Vera Rubin and Kent Ford, and then further developed by Rubin on her own, that dark matter was brought into the cosmological mainstream in 1969 and then throughout the 1970s. So who should get the credit for discovering dark matter?

TIFF: The Market exhibition booth option. At the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), which saw the inaugural edition of its official content market, the atmosphere was unmistakably different from its jubilee year. The spirit of nostalgic celebration and victory lapping from 2025's "TIFFty" celebration had evaporated, leaving behind the gritty residue of cinema as a commercial product. Lacking the elegance of “Marché du Film” at Cannes and the specificity of “European Film Market” at Berlinale, for their new industry initiative TIFF settled on a name that evokes the absurdity of local hero Matt Johnson’s Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (2025). Its sans-serif, all-lowercase stylization will transport some Canadians to the grocery aisle, recalling Loblaws mogul Galen Weston’s “No Name” brand, a proudly generic grocery chain that prides itself on serving its customer base during tough economic times (while price-gouging them to death). “TIFF: The Market” attempted to do the same, stimulating the global screen sector amid layoffs and mergers through a $16.

Jerónimo Quevedo is an Argentine producer and the founder of Un Puma, a production company through which he has produced more than twenty short, medium-length, and feature films spanning fiction, documentary, and experimental cinema. He has worked with both established and emerging directors from Latin America and Europe, including Martín Rejtman, Teddy Williams, Affonso Uchoa, Konstantina Kotzamani, Ico Costa, and Thomas Woodroffe. His filmography is characterized by projects that embrace significant artistic risks and a strong authorial vision, helping to renew the paths of Latin American cinema through works such as Teddy Williams’s The Human Surge (2016), Vladimir Durán’s Goodbye Enthusiasm (2017), Manque La Banc’s Ski (2021), and. Multiplex asks filmmakers, critics, and artists for short-form responses to the topic at hand. In this Halloween edition, contributors from around the world recommend one scary movie from their home country or region. Florian Widegger on West Germany Sukkubus—Den Teufel im Leib (Georg Tressler, 1989). What happens when a veteran director who helped shape postwar German-language cinema in the 1950s and ’60s decides to have one more go at it in his later years? When he casts two in-demand stage actors in the leading roles, alongside an Italian Playboy model whose physical assets steal the show? And when he draws on an old legend in which three shepherds, isolated in the Swiss Alps and frustrated by their forced sexual abstinence, fashion a female doll out of straw and roots? The answer is Sukkubus—Den Teufel im Leib (1989), an utterly bizarre mix of mountain drama, folk horror, and sexploitation in which the aforementioned doll comes to life and begins to hunt the men down.

Tender Buttons

MUBI Notebook · 2026-10-27 08:00 UTC

One Sings, the Other Doesn't (Agnès Varda, 1977). In her memoir, Varda par Agnès, the French director describes herself as “une féministe de terrain plus qu’une discuteuse,” roughly translated as “a feminist on the ground rather than in theory.” Later in the book, she describes the “feminists” discussing her work, implying that she was outside this group. How feminist she reads from any angle now is unclear. Many would, for instance, find her focus on the body and childbirth essentialist. Her 1975 short, Réponse de femmes: Notre corps, notre sexe (Women Reply: Our Bodies, Our Sex), opens with this prompt: “What does it mean to be a woman?” The text is painted on glass and held up by two women: “Qu’est ce qu’être femme?” While showing a naked female infant rolling around on its back, the reply comes in her voiceover: “To be born a woman means being born with female genitals.” The next shot is of a blond adult female, naked and standing up, saying, “To be a woman means inhabiting a woman’s body.

More Visible Abroad than at Home: Nigeria’s New Art Cinema and the Country that Can’t Screen It

MUBI Notebook · 2026-10-26 08:00 UTC

My Father's Shadow (Akinola Davies Jr., 2025). In Lagos last September, a handful of screenings of My Father’s Shadow (2025) played in theaters that were, depending on the night, half empty. A few months earlier, the same film had world premiered at Cannes, in the Un Certain Regard section, and walked away with a special mention for the Caméra d’Or. It was the first Nigerian film to be programmed in the official selection at the festival. Variety called Akinola Davies Jr.’s film miraculous. Rotten Tomatoes aggregated the critical assessment as 98% positive. However, there exists a cultural invisibility at home that stands against these genuine international recognitions. Despite all these nominations and recognitions, Nigerian audiences barely registered the film. I don’t think most Nigerians who heard about the Cannes win ever connected it to an actual cinema outing. But what is notable about this isn’t the story of one film not finding a local audience.

A Form of Utopianism: Cluster’s Sowiesoso at 50

The Quietus · 2026-11-02 08:00 UTC

From avant garde beginnings to ambient endings, Cluster reconfigured rock music as much as Kraftwerk, says Toby Manning. In the late 70s and early 80s, British music took a distinctly European turn, from Bowie’s “Heroes” in 1977 to Ultravox’s ‘Vienna’ in 1981, peaking with Kraftwerk’s ‘The Model’ hitting UK no. 1 the following year. Whether it was the after-effects of the EEC referendum or a growing anti-Americanism in the wake of Watergate and Vietnam, this new Europeanism temporarily sidelined music’s traditional Transatlantic passage for the artier terrain over the Channel. Chart hits like Visage’s ‘Fade To Grey’ in 1980, The Passions’ 1981 ‘I’m In Love With A German Film Star’, or The Mobiles’ ‘Drowning in Berlin’ from the same year were... Wire mix: Inside Prepared Piano

The Wire Magazine · 2026-10-27 00:00 UTC

To accompany her feature in The Wire 513, Jo Hutton compiles an annotated mix of tracks that make use of prepared piano The piano can be prepared by placing objects such as pins, screws, bolts, crocodile clips, ball bearings, kitchen utensils, magnets or tin foil on or between the strings. Its history dates back at least to the 1930s, when choreographer Syvilla Fort commissioned a dance piece from John Cage, who proposed his Bacchanale for percussion ensemble. But the performance theatre was too small to fit the intended ensemble, so Cage changed the sound of the house piano by adding screws and objects inside it to make it more percussive. This annotated mix includes tracks by some of the artists Jo Hutton speaks to as part of her feature in The Wire 513, plus pieces from across the history of the prepared piano.

culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe

Against The Grain: Metal resistance

The Wire Magazine · 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC

As far right ideology and misogyny make gains around the world, metal, a subculture with a troubled relationship to fascism, wonders whether more progressive ideals are still in reach, writes Antonio Poscic in The Wire 513 Metal used to be the music of outsiders. For teenagers who stumbled into it, the subculture offered a place to belong and legitimised intense emotions that had to be suppressed in daily life. Its lyrics and sonic density gave shape to alienation, despair and angst that many struggled to articulate. It offered acceptance for those rejected elsewhere, and an identity chosen rather than imposed. As sociologist Deena Weinstein’s research in the 1990s showed, metal circles often acted as scaffolding for adolescent development. Today, other subcultures have become fragmented by the internet and streaming, but metal remains a counterexample, perhaps precisely because of the strong sense of belonging on which it was built.

ArchDaily · 2026-11-02 06:30 UTC

In May 2024, the floods that hit Rio Grande do Sul exposed a contradiction common to contemporary cities. Many were built alongside rivers and shaped by their presence, yet spent decades trying to control water without incorporating its dynamics into urban planning. Extreme weather events will intensify that vulnerability. More than two years later, reconstruction in the Brazilian state has progressed, infrastructure has been restored, and new protection strategies are taking shape. But are these cities rebuilding their relationship with water, or only restoring the systems that failed?

"Nothing Starts From Zero": In Conversation With Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa of FADAA

ArchDaily · 2026-11-02 06:30 UTC

Following a seven-year pause, Amman Design Week returned in 2026 under the theme "Accumulations," bringing together designers, makers, and cultural practitioners to reflect on the work shaping Jordan's design landscape. The fourth edition, held from October 2 to 17, 2026, marked a new chapter for the event, with architects Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa, founders of the architecture and design practice FADAA, serving as co-directors. Their appointment also brought their research-driven approach to the event's broader program, which explored the relationships between daily practices, cultural memories, and material environments. During the event, we had the opportunity to speak with Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa about the thinking behind this year's theme, their approach to material investigations, and how practicing in Jordan informs their work across architecture, objects, and public space.

Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD to Transform a Mid-Century Warehouse into the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity

ArchDaily · 2026-11-02 05:30 UTC

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity has unveiled the masterplan for its forthcoming archives in Marin County, California. The project, designed by Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron and Bay Area-based EHDD, transforms a mid-century modern warehouse into a cultural destination, with art installation space, flexible galleries, learning and gathering spaces, a theater, and dining offerings. The large-scale adaptive reuse project is accompanied by a transformation of the gardens and grounds of the surrounding 88.5-acre site, led by Field Operations. While the Institute's Eames Archives will form one part of the museum, its exhibitions and programming are intended to extend far beyond the work of Charles and Ray Eames, bringing together different disciplines, creative processes, and ideas.

journal · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Accurate structural identification for layered composite structures, through a wave and finite element scheme

arXiv · 2026-11-02 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.40689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present for the first time an approach for identifying the geometric and material characteristics of layered composite structures through an inverse wave and finite element approach. More specifically, this Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE) approach is able to recover the thickness, density, as well as all independent mechanical characteristics such as the tensile and shear moduli for each layer of the composite structure under investigation. This is achieved through multi-frequency single shot measurements. It is emphasized that the success of the approach is independent of the employed excitation frequency regime, meaning that both structural dynamics and ultrasound frequency spectra can be employed. It is demonstrated that more efficient convergence of the identification process is attained closer to the bending-to-shear transition range of the layered structure. Since a full FE description is employed for the periodic composite, the presented approach is able to account for structures of arbitrary complexity.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

FLUCS: a modular GPU-native framework for fluid and plasma turbulence

arXiv · 2026-11-02 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.40794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present FLUCS, an open-source framework for solving systems of partial differential equations efficiently on graphics processing units (GPUs), targeting models of fluid and plasma turbulence. It comprises a set of numerical solvers specialised for a well-defined class of problems and independently developed systems that supply specific systems of equations. This allows different models to share numerical infrastructure while retaining control over their individual implementation and optimisation. The present release provides a Fourier pseudospectral solver for one-, two-, and three-dimensional periodic domains solved on a single NVIDIA GPU, with integrating-factor time integration and several time-stepping and dealiasing methods. We verify its convergence, quantify its computational costs, and demonstrate its application to three reduced models of fusion and astrophysical plasma turbulence.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods on Quantum Hardware

arXiv · 2026-11-02 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.40851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods encounter significant computational bottlenecks in large systems and at high Reynolds number flows due to the rapid increase in degrees of freedom, even on flagship supercomputers. As quantum computers emerge, the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has been proposed as a quantum-native alternative for solving fluid dynamics problems. However, until recently, nearly all studies have relied on classical quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware. This study presents a benchmark of a one-dimensional QLBM implementation executed on three different IBM Quantum hardware. We design and test a quantum circuit for the advection-diffusion equation using amplitude encoding, a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK)-type collision operator, and a streaming step with periodic boundary conditions.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Stress-enhanced diffusion in Yukawa crystals

arXiv · 2026-11-02 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.40892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-diffusion in crystallized Coulomb (Yukawa) plasmas proceeds by the thermally activated formation of vacancy-interstitial pairs and the migration of these defects through the lattice, commonly known as Frenkel pairs in the materials literature. Molecular dynamics has recently resolved an Eyring law for diffusion in unstrained crystals, which we generalize to deformed crystals in this work. We simulate sheared Yukawa crystals and show that a static elastic strain exponentially enhances diffusion due to the additional elastic energy stored in the region that participates in Frenkel pair formation relative to the unstrained crystal: $D(\varepsilon)=D_0(\Gamma^{*})\exp[V^{*}\sigma/k_{\rm B}T]$, with $\sigma=\tfrac12\mu\varepsilon^{2}$ the elastic energy density stored by the shear strain $\varepsilon$ and $V^{*}$ the activation volume. We find a single activation volume $N_{\rm act} = n_iV^{*}\simeq31$ suffices for typical astrophysical screenings with a reduction at higher screening.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Metadevices that compute: mathematical foundations and experimental implementations for neuromorphic nanophotonics

arXiv · 2026-11-02 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.40903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a compelling alternative to digital electronics for specific linear-algebraic and machine-learning workloads, promising massively parallel, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient information processing. Metamaterials, metasurfaces, and integrated metastructures (collectively, metadevices) now perform mathematical operations, solve integral and differential equations, multiply matrices, and implement trainable photonic neural networks directly in the wave domain. This focused review consolidates the mathematical foundations that underpin such devices, i.e., the mapping between linear operators and wave scattering, the feedback architectures that realize equation inversion, and the inverse-design and scientific machine-learning toolchains that make their synthesis and training tractable, and connects them to the rapidly growing body of experimental demonstrations, from free-space diffractive processors to reconfigurable guided-wave metastructures.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Construction and Commissioning of a Compact Xenon Gas Recycling System for a High-Harmonic Generation VUV Frequency Comb

arXiv · 2026-11-02 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.40923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A compact, closed-loop xenon recycling system for application in a High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) Vacuum-UV (VUV) frequency comb laser systems is designed, constructed and commissioned. It consists of three main sections, a low-pressure section (LPS) pre-filtering the gas of particulates, water and hydrocarbons, then a compression station (CS), allowing for a variable pressure of up to 60 bar, and a high-pressure section (HPS) with more filtering, pressure control and monitoring. The system proves to meet all design criteria in gas quality (the sum off all hydrocarbon contaminations up to 120 amu and CO$_{2}$ being below 10$^{-8}$ mbar) and recovery efficiency (>99.8$\%$ for all expected operational cases, neglecting possible geometric gas catcher losses in the HHG laser itself). The operation and results are presented and discussed. Furthermore, the system is compared to the performance of a similar system from which it is derived.

journal · primary · R5 · P5 · reference

Prognostic value of the preoperative C-reactive protein-to-lymphocyte ratio in patients with non-metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-10-30 14:00 UTC

by Minchao Qin, Zhongwen Feng, Chao Zhang, Wei Song, Kai Wang, Zhen Chen Background Systemic inflammation is associated with the prognosis of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). The C-reactive protein-to-lymphocyte ratio (CLR) combines systemic inflammation and host immune status. However, its prognostic value in non-metastatic ccRCC remains unclear. This study evaluated the association between preoperative CLR and survival outcomes in patients with non-metastatic ccRCC. Methods We retrospectively included 414 patients with non-metastatic ccRCC who underwent partial or radical nephrectomy. The primary Cox analyses treated ln(CLR) as a continuous variable and assessed overall survival (OS) and the cause-specific hazard of ccRCC-related death. Sensitivity analyses included expanded adjustment and time-varying effects. Cut-off-based analyses were exploratory. Time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves were used to compare CLR with other inflammatory markers. Incremental discrimination and calibration were assessed using bootstrap internal validation.

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Development of a competency framework for public health nurses in China: A modified Delphi study

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-10-30 14:00 UTC

by Chunxia He, Lingli Yan, Jia Yin, Qian Yao, Jiali Zhang, Jimei Zhang, Xiuying Hu Background Public health nurses play a pivotal role in primary public health services, yet China lacks a systematic, context-specific competency framework to support workforce development. This study aimed to develop a competency framework for public health nurses in China to guide capacity-building initiatives. Methods A preliminary competency framework was constructed based on a literature review, job analysis, and semi-structured interviews with 22 frontline practitioners and comprised six domains, 16 subdomains, and 52 competencies. A two-round Delphi survey was then conducted with 21 experts from multiple regions with expertise in community nursing, public health, primary care medicine, and nursing education and related specialties. Consensus was defined as a mean importance rating ≥4.0 (5-point Likert scale) and a coefficient of variation ≤0.25. The Delphi consultation process was characterized by expert engagement, the expert authority coefficient, and the coordination of expert opinions.

Detection of potentially curable recurrence after colorectal cancer surgery in a real-world population

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-10-30 14:00 UTC

by Ivonne J. H. Schoenaker, Richard M. Brohet, Evelyn J. Finnema, Dominique C. Damminga, Helle-Brit Fiebrich, Wouter H. de Vos tot Nederveen Cappel, Henderik L. van Westreenen Introduction After curative surgery for colorectal cancer (CRC), patients undergo surveillance because of the risk of recurrence; however, only a subset develops recurrence amenable to further curative-intent treatment. The primary aim of follow‑up is to identify patients with potentially curable recurrence. Materials and methods A retrospective analysis was performed of stage I–IV CRC patients who underwent curative-intent treatment and entered postoperative surveillance at Isala between 2014 and 2018. Follow‑up was conducted according to Dutch guideline‑based protocols for 60 months. Patients were categorized as having no recurrence, a potentially curable recurrence, or a non-curable recurrence. Prognostic factors at start of follow-up for potentially curable recurrence were assessed using competing‑risk Cox regression, with non-curable recurrence and death as competing events.

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Age-specific income losses due to HPV-attributable cancers in Singapore

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-10-30 14:00 UTC

by Robin Blythe, Nicholas Graves, N. Gopalakrishna Iyer, Marco A. Peres Introduction The link between Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and cancer is well-established. In Singapore, bivalent HPV vaccines are subsidised for females, but not males. Economic analysis of HPV vaccination has generally assessed the costs to the health system, but this may not be as relevant to individual decision-making as potential lost income. We estimated the impact of bivalent HPV 16/18 vaccination on sick leave, unemployment, and premature mortality as a function of age and sex to understand the broader impact of HPV-related cancers. Methods We developed a population-level economic model to estimate lifetime income losses by diagnosis age, sex and cancer type. We applied sex- and cancer-specific Cox regressions to the Singapore Cancer Registry for annual predicted survival from 1992 to 2022. These were combined with census and employment data to estimate HPV-associated income losses in Singapore.

[Comment] Redefining curative treatment for early-stage mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

For decades, the standard of care for patients with resected stage II and III colon cancer has centred on surgery with consideration of postoperative adjuvant systemic therapy to reduce risk of recurrence. Mismatch repair deficiency is seen in 10–15% of non-metastatic colon cancers and is predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibition. The initial report of the single-arm, phase 2 NICHE-2 study of one dose of ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) and two doses of nivolumab (3 mg per kg) before surgery with clinical stage II and III colon cancer generated considerable interest after demonstrating a remarkable 98% pathologic response rate, including a pathologic complete response rate of 68%.

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planet’s striking features, but the major difference is while Earth’s polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Mars’ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Mars’ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Mars’ climate history?

Ceres' Water Ice Can Mask Massive Surface Salt Deposits

Universe Today · 2026-10-31 23:35 UTC

The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an “asteroid” since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceres’ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceres’ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several “bright spots”, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceres’ formation and evolution?

Octopus and cuttlefish suckers may have evolved by repurposing ancient developmental genes

Phys.org Mollusks · 2026-10-20 13:30 UTC

Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

Rare Meteorite From Mars Gives Us A View Into Its Ancient Crust

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

"Arthur T knackerbracket" writes: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one. A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. "It's very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth," Liu says. [...] Teghaza 001 is made mostly of feldspar, a pale mineral common in the crusts of rocky planets. It has darker pyroxene crystals mixed in; according to Liu, those resemble some rocks exposed in the lunar highlands.

If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-01 23:24 UTC

I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-10-31 23:15 UTC

How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard, which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML, so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method.

specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Bliki: LLM Voice

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”.

Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?

TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right.

Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens. Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif. Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices. Same system, new voice At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu. A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines.

Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel

Vercel Blog · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations. Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate. Why we built Runtime Cache Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor. We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js.

Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-27 04:30 UTC

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions.

Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI

Netflix TechBlog · 2026-10-26 17:04 UTC

By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform

Netflix TechBlog · 2026-10-22 22:19 UTC

Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run.

Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-14 18:35 UTC

You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect. In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you begin You need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin.

The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.

Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward. At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration. Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left. Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right.

Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics / IEEE Spectrum · 2026-10-27 16:14 UTC

This article is brought to you by VicOne. A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation. At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

It was an early hint that their experiment might have been successful. NASA Wants More Than 70 Moon Landings in the Next Decade—But How?

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-12 15:27 UTC

At Firefly Aerospace in Texas, engineers have been doing what NASA’s chief, Jared Isaacman, likes to call “the near-impossible.” The Firefly team has been assembling Blue Ghost Mission 2, a robotic spacecraft intended to land on the far side of the moon in 2027. No U.S. spacecraft has ever gone there. Not very many have landed on the near side, either, for that matter. Blue Ghost 2 has thousands of potential failure points, and there is almost no room for error. Two ships sent by a competitor, Houston-based Intuitive Machines, reached the moon’s near side in 2024 and 2025 but fell over on landing and returned little useful data. In 2024, another mission, Peregrine Mission One, by Pittsburgh-based Astrobotic Technology, missed the moon entirely because a single helium valve wouldn’t seat properly. In summary: Moon landings are supremely hard. So far, since Project Apollo ended in 1972, U.S. spacecraft have landed intact exactly…once.

Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

IEEE Spectrum · 2026-11-01 14:00 UTC

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship.

When Electric Cars Were for Women

IEEE Spectrum · 2026-10-31 13:00 UTC

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000. For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.
